title: Find the Town Judge
prompt:
In a town of `n` people labeled `1` to `n`, there might exist a town judge. You are given an array `trust` where `trust[i] = [a, b]` means person `a` trusts person `b`. The town judge, if it exists, is the one person who trusts nobody, but is trusted by every other person in town.

Return the label of the town judge if such a person exists and can be identified, or `-1` otherwise.

examples.explanation: Person 1 trusts person 2, and person 2 trusts nobody, so person 2 is the judge.
Person 3 trusts person 1, so person 3 cannot be the judge, and no one else qualifies either.
With only one person and no trust relationships, that person trivially trusts nobody and is trusted by everybody else (there is nobody else), so they are the judge.

constraints: All the pairs of trust are unique
hints: Checking every candidate against every trust pair directly would be O(n * trust.length) — think about what property a 'trusts everyone else, trusted by no one' node has in terms of edges.
Model this as a directed graph: an edge a -> b means a trusts b. Track each person's out-degree (how many people they trust) and in-degree (how many people trust them).
The judge, if one exists, is the unique person with out-degree exactly 0 and in-degree exactly n - 1. Compute both degree arrays in a single pass over trust.

solution.approach: Treat trust pairs as directed edges and maintain a single net score per person: increment the score of the trusted person and decrement the score of the truster. A person who trusts no one and is trusted by everyone else ends up with a net score of exactly n - 1, and no one else can reach that value (trusting even one person costs you at least one point). Scan the score array for a person whose score equals n - 1.
